candidates.name: Let Your Team Hire Their Own Team
candidates.mechanism: Referral bonuses alone don't move the needle much on how many people apply. What a referral program really changes is how existing employees feel about the workplace: being trusted enough to vouch for someone makes them more invested and likely to stay, whether or not their own referral actually gets hired.
candidates.evidence: A randomized study of employee referral programs rolled out across a grocery chain (NBER Working Paper 25920) found the programs reduced overall staff attrition by 15% and lowered labor costs — driven mainly not by the referred hires themselves, but by existing employees at stores with the program staying longer, because they felt more involved in hiring.
candidates.transferTemplate: Put a real, visible referral bonus behind 'know a good tech?' — but treat it as more than a recruiting tactic. The bigger effect isn't the new hire it produces, it's that your current crew feels like their judgment about who's good enough to join the team actually matters. That sense of ownership is what keeps your existing techs around, not just the people they referred.

candidates.name: Build the Trade, Don't Just Hire For It
candidates.mechanism: When the labor market for a skill is thin, competing for already-trained people is a losing game everyone is playing at once. Training your own apprentices from scratch, with a real pathway and paid learning time, creates a pipeline nobody else is fishing in and builds loyalty because the company invested in them first.
candidates.evidence: Aon retains 80% of its apprentices, and the U.S. Department of Labor found employers see roughly a 44.3% return on investment from registered apprenticeship programs overall.
candidates.transferTemplate: Instead of only competing for already-licensed techs against every other shop in town, build a real apprentice pathway: paid on-the-job training, a defined timeline to full pay, and a named mentor. It costs more upfront than just hiring, but it fills a role competitors are all bidding for the same tiny pool to fill, and apprentices who were trained in-house tend to stay because the company is where they actually learned the trade.

candidates.name: Widen the Pool by Removing a Filter Nobody Re-Examines
candidates.mechanism: Many employers default to screening out an entire pool of otherwise-capable candidates — most commonly, anyone with a criminal record — without ever re-testing whether that filter is actually protecting them or just shrinking an already-thin labor pool. Deliberately hiring from a pool competitors ignore can fill roles that would otherwise sit open for months.
candidates.evidence: Dave's Killer Bread built roughly one in three employees at its headquarters from people with criminal records, and its training program teaching other employers how to do the same scaled to over 34 companies — including Dick's Sporting Goods, General Motors, and Union Pacific Railroad — before Jobs for the Future acquired it to scale further. Separately, a national SHRM survey found 66% of HR professionals report their organizations have hired people with criminal records, and the U.S. Chamber of Commerce found employers who do this see lower turnover and higher motivation among those hires.
candidates.transferTemplate: If you're consistently short on applicants, look at whether a blanket policy (an automatic 'no' on any criminal record, a strict experience minimum, a specific certification you could train for instead) is filtering out people who could actually do the job well. Loosening a filter that isn't truly load-bearing for safety or licensing opens up a pool of motivated candidates that most of your competitors are still screening out by default.
